reading.title: Words That Do Two Jobs
reading.purpose: Discover how one everyday English word can carry two or three different meanings.
paras: English is full of clever words that do more than one job. To know which meaning fits, you have to read the words around it like a detective.

Take the word trunk. In a park, a trunk is the thick wooden stem of a tree. At a zoo, a trunk is an elephant's long nose. On a road trip, you pack bags in the trunk at the back of a car. The word palm works the same way: it can mean the inside of your hand, or a tall leafy tree on a warm beach.

Other words shift from one setting to another. A scale can weigh apples at a store, cover a fish like tiny plates, or rise in musical notes. You can pitch a baseball to a catcher, or pitch a tent at camp. You can charge forward like a bull, charge a phone battery, or ask what a shop will charge for a hat.

Even school and story words pull double duty. A pupil is a student at a desk, and also the dark circle in the middle of your eye. A firm mattress is hard to press, while a firm promise will not change. A duck eats with its bill, and a diner pays a bill. You can tie a ribbon bow, take a bow after a play, or cast a magic spell during a rainy spell.
Next time a word surprises you, check the whole sentence to see which job it is doing.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, what are two meanings of the word "pupil"?
choices: a student at school and the dark circle in the eye
a ribbon tied in a neat knot and a bend of the body
a tall tree on a warm beach and the inside of a hand
a hard mattress on a bed and a strong promise
qs.why: Paragraph 4 states that a pupil is "a student at a desk, and also the dark circle in the middle of your eye."

qs.q: Which sentence gives three different ways to use the word "scale"?
choices: Other words shift from one setting to another.
A scale can weigh apples at a store, cover a fish like tiny plates, or rise in musical notes.
You can pitch a baseball to a catcher, or pitch a tent at camp.
A duck eats with its bill, and a diner pays a bill.
qs.why: This sentence lists weighing apples, fish plates, and musical notes as three uses of scale.

ev.text: A scale can weigh apples at a store, cover a fish like tiny plates, or rise in musical notes.

qs.q: A waiter sets a paper on the table showing that lunch costs twelve dollars. Which word from the reading names that paper?
qs.why: Paragraph 4 explains that a diner pays a bill, which is the paper showing what is owed.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Words like trunk and palm are too confusing for young readers to learn well.
Many English words have multiple meanings, and the sentence shows which one fits.
Baseball games and camping trips always use the exact same set of vocabulary words.
Every word in English has at least three completely different meanings in a dictionary.
qs.why: The passage gives examples of multi-meaning words and advises readers to check the whole sentence to see which meaning fits.

clues.text: the thick wooden stem of a tree
